analysis.one_liner: Boosts Social Security benefits for retirees, low earners, and students, and pays for it with taxes on high incomes and investments.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2021 with zero cosponsors and died in committee without ever receiving a vote in the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise every future Social Security check by up to 15%, raise cost-of-living adjustments using an index that better reflects what seniors actually buy, guarantee a minimum benefit near the poverty line for people who worked at least 10-30 years, and let children of disabled or deceased workers keep benefits until age 22 while in school. To pay for it, Social Security payroll taxes would apply to income above $250,000 (today earnings past roughly $143,000 are exempt) and the tax on investment income would more than double from 3.8% to 10.2%. It would also merge the retirement and disability trust funds into one. It never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries, especially low-earning retirees and disabled workers who would get a guaranteed minimum benefit at or above the poverty line; seniors generally, whose cost-of-living adjustments would rise faster under an elderly-focused inflation index; and children of disabled or deceased workers in school, who could keep benefits to age 22. Social Security itself would gain a longer-lasting financing base.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, disabled workers, and low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises every future Social Security check above today's levels, phasing in a 1-percentage-point-per-year increase starting in 2027 until it reaches 15% higher in 2041 and after.

Establishes a new minimum benefit for lifetime low earners, scaling up to 125% of the federal poverty guideline for those with 30 or more years of work, directly lifting the poorest retirees and disabled workers.
Switches the cost-of-living adjustment to the CPI for Elderly Consumers, which better tracks the higher inflation seniors face on health care and housing.
Lets children of retired, deceased, or disabled workers keep receiving benefits until age 22 while in school full time, instead of cutting them off around 18-19.

Extends Social Security payroll taxes to earnings above $250,000 and raises the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 10.2%, directing the new revenue to the trust fund to keep benefits payable for the long term.

analysis.who_pays: High-income households: people with wage or self-employment income above $250,000 would pay Social Security payroll tax on the excess, and investors with net investment income would see that tax rise from 3.8% to 10.2%. Anyone earning under $250,000 in wages pays nothing new.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 10.2% and applies payroll taxes above $250,000, which critics of such proposals say would raise taxes on professionals, small-business owners, and investors and could discourage work and investment above the threshold.

Because the benefit increases phase in over more than a decade and the financing depends on future tax collections, the long-term actuarial math would depend on economic assumptions; the bill itself requires new actuarial analysis of the combined fund rather than guaranteeing the projection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and targeted: higher checks for retirees, a minimum benefit near the poverty line for low-wage workers, better inflation protection, and longer support for students. The costs fall on households above $250,000 in earnings and on investment income, and the financing is designed to improve solvency rather than rely on borrowed money. The main honest objection is that the 10.2% NIIT and the new payroll tax above $250,000 could reduce incentives to work and invest, and that phasing benefits up while phasing in taxes leaves little cushion if revenue falls short of projections. On the whole it is a solvent, progressive expansion rather than an unfunded one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to three House committees, including Ways and Means, and none of them ever acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on September 10, 2021.
The same day it was referred to the Ways and Means, Education and Labor, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees, and within days to their Social Security and rail subcommittees.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without any further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with income above $250,000 and high-income investors, who would have faced the new payroll-tax and investment-tax burdens, are better off because it never moved; low-income seniors and disabled workers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors, not beneficiaries

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand Social Security benefits and finance them with taxes on high earnings and investment income.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of jurisdiction over Social Security
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote; it remained in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: High-income taxpayers and the financial industry
against.role: Groups whose investment income and high earnings the bill would tax
against.what_they_did: Generally opposed expansions of payroll and investment taxes; opposition groups consistently lobbied against lifting the payroll tax cap and raising the net investment income tax during this period.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no recorded votes, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.industry: High-earning professionals and self-employed people (income above $250,000)
industries.note: Their wages and business income above $250,000 would become subject to Social Security payroll tax for the first time.
The net investment income tax on capital gains and investment income rises from 3.8% to 10.2%, a direct new cost on investment earnings flowing to Social Security.

industries.industry: Retirees, disabled workers, survivors, and their children
industries.note: Not an industry, but the group the bill is built around: they gain higher benefits, a poverty-level minimum, and longer student-child coverage, paid for by the taxes above.
